title: Linear Momentum
short_intro: Linear momentum is a vector quantity defined as the product of an object's mass and its velocity. It serves as a measure of the quantity of motion contained in a translational body.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, units, dimensions, vector nature, conservation of linear momentum in one and two dimensions, application to recoil of guns, collisions in a straight line (elastic and inelastic).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Generalization to systems of many particles, relationship with Newton's second law in differential and integral forms, impulse-momentum theorem, variable mass systems (rocket propulsion).

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Vector Nature
bullets: Linear momentum p is defined as p = mv, where m is the inertial mass and v is the velocity vector.
It has the dimensions [M L T^-1] and SI units of kilogram meter per second (kg m/s) or Newton-second (N s).
The direction of the linear momentum vector is always identical to the direction of the instantaneous velocity vector.

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Second Law and Momentum
bullets: Newton's second law states that the external force acting on a particle equals the time rate of change of its linear momentum: F_ext = dp/dt.
When the mass m remains constant, this relation reduces to the familiar form F = ma.
If the net external force acting on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains conserved (constant).

concept_notes.heading: Impulse of a Force
bullets: Impulse J is defined as the integral of force over the time interval for which it acts: J = integral of F dt.
According to the impulse-momentum theorem, the total impulse imparted to an object equals the net change in its linear momentum: J = Delta p.
In graphs of force versus time, the area under the curve represents the linear impulse delivered to the system.

concept_notes.heading: Conservation of Linear Momentum in Systems
bullets: For an isolated system of N interacting particles, internal forces sum to zero by Newton's third law.
The total linear momentum P = sum of p_i remains strictly conserved in the absence of net external forces.
This principle is independent of the nature of internal forces, whether conservative (like springs or gravity) or non-conservative (like friction).

derivations.title: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
derivations.conditions: Force acting over a time interval t_1 to t_2
steps: Start from Newton's second law: F = dp/dt.
Rearrange the differential expression: dp = F dt.
Integrate both sides from initial state (t_1, p_1) to final state (t_2, p_2): Delta p = integral from t_1 to t_2 of F dt.

derivations.title: Rocket Propulsion Equation (Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation)
derivations.conditions: Variable mass system moving in free space with no external forces
steps: Write the initial momentum of the rocket at time t: p(t) = m(t)v(t).
At time t + dt, the mass becomes m + dm (where dm is negative) and velocity becomes v + dv. The ejected mass leaves with relative exhaust velocity v_rel.
Apply conservation of linear momentum: m(t)v(t) = (m + dm)(v + dv) + (-dm)(v - v_rel).
Expand, drop second-order differentials (dm dv), and integrate from initial mass m_0 to m and initial velocity v_0 to v.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force vs. Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing force on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed between the curve and the time axis represents the impulse delivered to the body during that time interval.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual questions asking to calculate change in momentum from graphical areas.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Momentum vs. Velocity Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin for a constant mass particle.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line graph gives the inertial mass (m = p/v) of the object.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identifying physical properties from experimental slope interpretations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ballistic Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a bullet striking and embedding into a suspended block, causing a vertical rise h.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Combines the conservation of linear momentum during the collision with the conservation of mechanical energy during the subsequent swing.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard apparatus-based problem testing simultaneous application of momentum and energy conservation.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 2 kg moving with a velocity of 3 m/s collides head-on with another body of mass 3 kg moving in the opposite direction with a velocity of 2 m/s. If the two bodies stick together after the collision, what is their common velocity?
solution_steps: Let the initial direction of the 2 kg mass be positive. Then u_1 = +3 m/s, m_1 = 2 kg.
The second body moves in the opposite direction, so u_2 = -2 m/s, m_2 = 3 kg.
Apply conservation of linear momentum: m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v.

solved_numericals.question: A rocket has an initial mass of 1000 kg including 800 kg of fuel. It consumes fuel at a constant rate of 10 kg/s and the relative speed of exhaust gases is 2000 m/s. Find the thrust developed by the rocket and its acceleration at the end of 50 seconds, neglecting external gravitational force.
solution_steps: Thrust force is given by F_thrust = v_rel * (dm/dt).
Substitute v_rel = 2000 m/s and dm/dt = 10 kg/s: F_thrust = 2000 * 10 = 20000 N.
Calculate mass of the rocket at t = 50 s: m(t) = m_0 - (rate)*t = 1000 - (10 * 50) = 500 kg.
Apply Newton's second law for acceleration: a = F_thrust / m(t) = 20000 / 500 = 40 m/s^2.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass m moving with velocity v breaks into two fragments of masses m/3 and 2m/3 due to an internal explosion. If the fragment of mass m/3 comes to rest, find the velocity of the second fragment.
solution_steps: Initial momentum of the system is p_i = m v.
Let the velocity of the second fragment of mass 2m/3 be v'.
Final momentum of the system is p_f = (m/3)(0) + (2m/3)v'.
By conservation of linear momentum, p_i = p_f: m v = (2m/3)v'.
solved_numericals.answer: 3v/2 in the original direction of motion

assumptions_and_limitations: Conservation of linear momentum strictly applies to isolated systems where net external force is zero; in non-inertial frames, pseudoforces must be accounted for.
Classical expressions for momentum (p = mv) fail when particle speeds approach the speed of light, requiring relativistic formulations p = gamma m v.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Kinetic energy is always conserved in any collision where linear momentum is conserved.
common_misconceptions.correct: Linear momentum is conserved in all collisions in the absence of external forces, whereas kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions.
common_misconceptions.why: In inelastic collisions, mechanical energy is dissipated into heat, sound, or deformation work while momentum remains conserved.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the net external force on a system is zero, individual particles within the system cannot change their momentum.
common_misconceptions.correct: Individual particles can experience large changes in internal momentum due to internal forces.
common_misconceptions.why: Conservation applies only to the vector sum of momenta of all particles, not to individual components.
